newsitem.title: USA: U.S. analyst suggests "Freedom to Farm" successor.
newsitem.headline: U.S. analyst suggests "Freedom to Farm" successor.

text.p: The successor to the "Freedom to Farm" law should be a U.S.-backed insurance plan that protects farm income, a more effective and straightforward approach than crop insurance, a private analyst said Thursday.

During a luncheon with reporters, Carole Brookins described her proposed Farm Production Insurance Corp (FPIC) as "son of Freedom to Farm" and "the next phase" in giving farmers the tools to manage risk as the federal role in agriculture shrinks.
Brookins is founder and chairman of World Perspectives Inc, an agricultural analysis and consulting firm.

FPIC would be an independent federal agency that sold insurance coverage on a farm's gross production revenue. Livestock would be eligible for coverage as well as crops. Maximum benefit would be capped at $250,000.

"It's just at the policy stage," Brookins said, saying an actuarial analysis has yet to be done. Nonetheless, she said FPIC should be less costly than the variations of crop insurance now on the market and underwritten by the Federal Crop Insurance Corp.

The Clinton adminstration has proposed making revenue insurance, which protects farmers against steep declines in yields and market prices, available nationwide. But questions have been raised about its potential cost.
Brookins said FPIC was simpler and more direct because it would be based on a farm's sales revenue.
Payment would be triggered when revenue from farm production fell more than 50 percent. Farmers could buy insurance or use other techniques to protect against smaller losses.

A provision of the Freedom to Farm law calls for the appointment later this year of an 11-member Commission on 21st Century Production Agriculture to suggest farm policy after 2002. Brookins said proposal of FPIC might stimulate discussion of the most efficient way to assure food security.
"The issue is, what are we trying to do. We have not had that debate," she said.
Another private consultant said Brookins might be premature in floating her plan years before Freedom to Farm expires.
"I don't think it's time to talk about a replacement for Freedom to Farm payments, which are going swimmingly," said the consultant, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
